entries.11d234ded88cf88e9dbcaf9ef9198eecf6d2bcc0: <div sID="gen18118" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="46" osisID="Jer.46" sID="Jer.46"/> <div eID="gen18118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18119" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18120" type="x-p"/> How judgment began at the house of God we have found in the foregoing prophecy and history; but now we shall find that it did not end there. In this and the following chapters we have predictions of the desolations of the neighbouring nations, and those brought upon them too mostly by the king of Babylon, till at length Babylon itself comes to be reckoned with. The prophecy against Egypt is here put first and takes up this whole chapter, in which we have, I. A prophecy of the defeat of Pharaoh-necho's army by the Chaldean forces at Carchemish, which was accomplished soon after, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.1-Jer.46.12">ver. 1-12</reference>. II. A prophecy of the descent which Nebuchadnezzar should make upon the land of Egypt, and his success in it, which was accomplished some years after the destruction of Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.13-Jer.46.26">ver. 13-26</reference>. III. A word of comfort to the Israel of God in the midst of those calamities, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.27-Jer.46.28">ver. 27, 28</reference>.
entries.ed1590b234463ed224afeeb6e813bef0d570df3d: <div eID="gen18120" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18119" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Judgment of Egypt. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 608.)</title> <div sID="gen18121" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> which came to Jeremiah the prophet against the Gentiles; <hi type="super">2</hi> Against Egypt, against the army of Pharaoh-necho king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates in Carchemish, which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon smote in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah. <hi type="super">3</hi> Order ye the buckler and shield, and draw near to battle. <hi type="super">4</hi> Harness the horses; and get up, ye horsemen, and stand forth with <hi type="italic">your</hi> helmets; furbish the spears, <hi type="italic">and</hi> put on the brigandines. <hi type="super">5</hi> Wherefore have I seen them dismayed <hi type="italic">and</hi> turned away back? and their mighty ones are beaten down, and are fled apace, and look not back: <hi type="italic">for</hi> fear <hi type="italic">was</hi> round about, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">6</hi> Let not the swift flee away, nor the mighty man escape; they shall stumble, and fall toward the north by the river Euphrates. <hi type="super">7</hi> Who <hi type="italic">is</hi> this <hi type="italic">that</hi> cometh up as a flood, whose waters are moved as the rivers? <hi type="super">8</hi> Egypt riseth up like a flood, and <hi type="italic">his</hi> waters are moved like the rivers; and he saith, I will go up, <hi type="italic">and</hi> will cover the earth; I will destroy the city and the inhabitants thereof. <hi type="super">9</hi> Come up, ye horses; and rage, ye chariots; and let the mighty men come forth; the Ethiopians and the Libyans, that handle the shield; and the Lydians, that handle <hi type="italic">and</hi> bend the bow. <hi type="super">10</hi> For this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the day of the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> of hosts, a day of vengeance, that he may avenge him of his adversaries: and the sword shall devour, and it shall be satiate and made drunk with their blood: for the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> of hosts hath a sacrifice in the north country by the river Euphrates. <hi type="super">11</hi> Go up into Gilead, and take balm, O virgin, the daughter of Egypt: in vain shalt thou use many medicines; <hi type="italic">for</hi> thou shalt not be cured. <div eID="gen18121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18122" type="x-p"/> The first verse is the title of that part of this book, which relates to the neighbouring nations, and follows here. It is <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord which came to Jeremiah against the Gentiles;</hi> for God is King and Judge of nations, knows and will call to an account those who know him not nor take any notice of him. Both Isaiah and Ezekiel prophesied against these nations that Jeremiah here has a separate saying to, and with reference to the same events. In the Old Testament we have <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord</hi> against <hi type="italic">the Gentiles;</hi> in the New Testament we have <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord</hi> for <hi type="italic">the Gentiles,</hi> that those who were <hi type="italic">afar off are made nigh.</hi> <div eID="gen18122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18123" type="x-p"/> He begins with Egypt, because they were of old Israel's oppressors and of late their deceivers, when they put confidence in them. In these verses he foretells the overthrow of <hi type="italic">the army of Pharaoh-necho,</hi> by Nebuchadnezzar, <hi type="italic">in the fourth year of Jehoiakim,</hi> which was so complete a victory to the king of Babylon that thereby he recovered from the river of Egypt to <hi type="italic">the river Euphrates, all that pertained to the king of Egypt,</hi> and so weakened him that he <hi type="italic">came not again any more out of his land</hi> (as we find, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.7">2 Kings xxiv. 7</reference>), and so made him pay dearly for his expedition against the king of Assyria four years before, in which he slew Josiah, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.29">2 Kings xxiii. 29</reference>. This is the event that is here foretold in lofty expressions of triumph over Egypt thus foiled, which Jeremiah would speak of with a particular pleasure, because the death of Josiah, which he had lamented, was now avenged on Pharaoh-necho. Now here, <div eID="gen18123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18124" type="x-p"/> I. The Egyptians are upbraided with the mighty preparations they made for this expedition, in which the prophet calls to them to do their utmost, for so they would: "Come then, <hi type="italic">order the buckler,</hi> let the weapons of war be got ready," <reference osisRef="Jer.46.3">v. 3</reference>. Egypt was famous for <hi type="italic">horses</hi>—let them be <hi type="italic">harnessed</hi> and the cavalry well mounted: <hi type="italic">Get up, you horsemen, and stand forth,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Jer.46.4">v. 4</reference>. See what preparations the children of men make, with abundance of care and trouble and at a vast expense, to kill one another, as if they did not die fast enough of themselves. He compares their marching out upon this expedition to the rising of their river Nile (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.7-Jer.46.8">v. 7, 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Egypt</hi> now <hi type="italic">rises up like a flood,</hi> scorning to keep within its own banks and threatening to overflow all the neighbouring lands. It is a very formidable army that the Egyptians bring into the field upon this occasion. The prophet summons them (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Come up, you horses; rage, you chariots.</hi> He challenges them to bring all their confederate troops together, <hi type="italic">the Ethiopians,</hi> that descended from the same stock with the Egyptians (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.6">Gen. x. 6</reference>), and were their neighbours and allies, <hi type="italic">the Libyans and Lydians,</hi> both seated in Africa, to the west of Egypt, and from them the Egyptians fetched their auxiliary forces. Let them strengthen themselves with all the art and interest they have, yet it shall be all in vain; they shall be shamefully defeated notwithstanding, for God will fight against them, and against him <hi type="italic">there is no wisdom nor counsel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.30-Prov.21.31">Prov. xxi. 30, 31</reference>. It concerns those that go forth to war not only to <hi type="italic">order the buckler,</hi> and <hi type="italic">harness the horses,</hi> but to repent of their sins, and pray to God for his presence with them, and that they may have it to keep themselves from every wicked thing. <div eID="gen18124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18125" type="x-p"/> II. They are upbraided with the great expectations they had from this expedition, which were quite contrary to what God intended in bringing them together. They knew their own thoughts, and God knew them, and sat in heaven and laughed at them; <hi type="italic">but they knew not the thoughts of the Lord, for he gathers them as sheaves into the floor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.4.11-Mic.4.12">Mic. iv. 11, 12</reference>. Egypt saith (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will go up; I will cover the earth,</hi> and none shall hinder me; <hi type="italic">I will destroy the city,</hi> whatever city it is that stands in my way. Like Pharaoh of old, <hi type="italic">I will pursue, I will overtake.</hi> The Egyptians say that they shall have a day of it, but God saith that it shall be his day: <hi type="italic">The is the day of the Lord God of hosts</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.10">v. 10</reference>), the day in which he will be exalted in the overthrow of the Egyptians. They meant one thing, but God meant another; they designed it for the advancement of their dignity and the enlargement of their dominion, but God designed it for the great abasement and weakening of their kingdom. It is <hi type="italic">a day of vengeance</hi> for Josiah's death; it is a day of sacrifice to divine justice, to which multitudes of the sinners of Egypt shall fall as victims. Note, When men think to magnify themselves by pushing on unrighteous enterprises, let them expect that God will glorify himself by blasting them and cutting them off. <div eID="gen18125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18126" type="x-p"/> III. They are upbraided with their cowardice and inglorious flight when they come to an engagement (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.5-Jer.46.6">v. 5, 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Wherefore have I seen them,</hi> notwithstanding all these mighty and vast preparations and all these expressions of bravery and resolution, when the Chaldean army faces them, <hi type="italic">dismayed, turned back,</hi> quite disheartened, and no spirit left in them." 1. They make a shameful retreat. Even <hi type="italic">their mighty ones,</hi> who, one would think, should have stood their ground, <hi type="italic">flee a flight,</hi> flee by consent, make the best of their way, flee in confusion and with the utmost precipitation; they have neither time nor heart to <hi type="italic">look back,</hi> but <hi type="italic">fear is round about</hi> them, for they apprehend it so. And yet, 2. They cannot make their escape. They have the shame of flying, and yet not the satisfaction of saving themselves by flight; they might as well have stood their ground and died upon the spot; for even <hi type="italic">the swift shall not flee away.</hi> The lightness of their heels shall fail them when it comes to the trial, as well as the stoutness of their hearts; the <hi type="italic">mighty</hi> shall not escape, nay, they <hi type="italic">are beaten down</hi> and broken to pieces. <hi type="italic">They shall stumble</hi> in their flight, <hi type="italic">and fall towards the north,</hi> towards their enemy's country; for such confusion were they in when they took to their feet that instead of making homeward, as men usually do in that case, they made forward. Note, <hi type="italic">The race is not to the swift nor the battle to the strong.</hi> Valiant men are not always victorious. <div eID="gen18126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18127" type="x-p"/> IV. They are upbraided with their utter inability ever to recover this blow, which should be fatal to their nation, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.11-Jer.46.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. The damsel, <hi type="italic">the daughter of Egypt,</hi> that lived in great pomp and state, is sorely wounded by this defeat. Let her now seek for <hi type="italic">balm in Gilead</hi> and physicians there; let her use all the medicines her wise men can prescribe for the healing of this hurt, and the repairing of the loss sustained by this defeat; but all in vain; <hi type="italic">no cure shall be</hi> to them; they shall never be able to bring such a powerful army as this into the field again. "<hi type="italic">The nations</hi> that rang of thy glory and strength <hi type="italic">have</hi> now <hi type="italic">heard of thy shame,</hi> how shamefully thou wast routed and how thou are weakened by it." It needs not be spread by the triumphs of the conquerors, the shrieks and outcries of the conquered will proclaim it: <hi type="italic">Thy cry hath filled the</hi> country about. For, when they fled several ways, one <hi type="italic">mighty man stumbled</hi> upon another and dashed against another, such confusion were they in, so that <hi type="italic">both together</hi> became a prey to the pursuers, an easy prey. A thousand such dreadful accidents there should be, which should fill the country with the cry of those that were overcome. <hi type="italic">Let not the mighty man</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">glory in his might,</hi> for the time may come when it will stand him in no stead.
entries.24909f1b30339bd9192bc2a479692668ed2339b1: <div eID="gen18127" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Judgment of Egypt. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 608.)</title> <div sID="gen18128" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> The nations have heard of thy shame, and thy cry hath filled the land: for the mighty man hath stumbled against the mighty, <hi type="italic">and</hi> they are fallen both together. <hi type="super">13</hi> The word that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake to Jeremiah the prophet, how Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon should come <hi type="italic">and</hi> smite the land of Egypt. <hi type="super">14</hi> Declare ye in Egypt, and publish in Migdol, and publish in Noph and in Tahpanhes: say ye, Stand fast, and prepare thee; for the sword shall devour round about thee. <hi type="super">15</hi> Why are thy valiant <hi type="italic">men</hi> swept away? they stood not, because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> did drive them. <hi type="super">16</hi> He made many to fall, yea, one fell upon another: and they said, Arise, and let us go again to our own people, and to the land of our nativity, from the oppressing sword. <hi type="super">17</hi> They did cry there, Pharaoh king of Egypt <hi type="italic">is but</hi> a noise; he hath passed the time appointed. <hi type="super">18</hi> <hi type="italic">As</hi> I live, saith the King, whose name <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, Surely as Tabor <hi type="italic">is</hi> among the mountains, and as Carmel by the sea, <hi type="italic">so</hi> shall he come. <hi type="super">19</hi> O thou daughter dwelling in Egypt, furnish thyself to go into captivity: for Noph shall be waste and desolate without an inhabitant. <hi type="super">20</hi> Egypt <hi type="italic">is like</hi> a very fair heifer, <hi type="italic">but</hi> destruction cometh; it cometh out of the north. <hi type="super">21</hi> Also her hired men <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the midst of her like fatted bullocks; for they also are turned back, <hi type="italic">and</hi> are fled away together: they did not stand, because the day of their calamity was come upon them, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the time of their visitation. <hi type="super">22</hi> The voice thereof shall go like a serpent; for they shall march with an army, and come against her with axes, as hewers of wood. <hi type="super">23</hi> They shall cut down her forest, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , though it cannot be searched; because they are more than the grasshoppers, and <hi type="italic">are</hi> innumerable. <hi type="super">24</hi> The daughter of Egypt shall be confounded; she shall be delivered into the hand of the people of the north. <hi type="super">25</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel, saith; Behold, I will punish the multitude of No, and Pharaoh, and Egypt, with their gods, and their kings; even Pharaoh, and <hi type="italic">all</hi> them that trust in him: <hi type="super">26</hi> And I will deliver them into the hand of those that seek their lives, and into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and into the hand of his servants: and afterward it shall be inhabited, as in the days of old, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">27</hi> But fear not thou, O my servant Jacob, and be not dismayed, O Israel: for, behold, I will save thee from afar off, and thy seed from the land of their captivity; and Jacob shall return, and be in rest and at ease, and none shall make <hi type="italic">him</hi> afraid. <hi type="super">28</hi> Fear thou not, O Jacob my servant, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> with thee; for I will make a full end of all the nations whither I have driven thee: but I will not make a full end of thee, but correct thee in measure; yet will I not leave thee wholly unpunished. <div eID="gen18128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18129" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen18129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18130" type="x-p"/> I. Confusion and terror spoken to Egypt. The accomplishment of the prediction in the former part of the chapter disabled the Egyptians from making any attempts upon other nations; for what could they do when their army was routed? But still they remained strong at home, and none of their neighbours durst make any attempts upon them. Though the kings of Egypt came no more <hi type="italic">out of their land</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.7">2 Kings xxiv. 7</reference>), yet they kept safe and easy in their land; and what would they desire more than peaceably to enjoy their own? One would think all men should be content to do this, and not covet to invade their neighbours. But the measure of Egypt's iniquity is full, and now they shall not long enjoy their own; those that encroached on others shall not be themselves encroached on. The scope of the prophecy here is to show <hi type="italic">how the king of Babylon should</hi> shortly <hi type="italic">come and smite the land of Egypt,</hi> and bring the war into their own bosoms which they had formerly carried into his borders, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.13">v. 13</reference>. This was fulfilled by the same hand with the former, even Nebuchadnezzar's, but many years after, twenty at least, and probably the prediction of it was long after the former prediction, and perhaps much about the same time with that other prediction of the same event which we had <reference osisRef="Jer.43.10">ch. xliii. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen18130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18131" type="x-p"/> 1. Here is the alarm of war sounded in Egypt, to their great amazement (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.14">v. 14</reference>), notice given to the country that the enemy is approaching, <hi type="italic">the sword is devouring round about</hi> in the neighbouring countries, and therefore it is time for the Egyptians to put themselves in a posture of defence, to prepare for war, that they may give the enemy a warm reception. This must be proclaimed in all parts of Egypt, particularly in Migdol, Noph, and Tahpanhes, because in these places especially the Jewish refugees, or fugitives rather, had planted themselves, in contempt of God's command (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.1">ch. xliv. 1</reference>), and let them hear what a sorry shelter Egypt is likely to be to them. <div eID="gen18131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18132" type="x-p"/> 2. The retreat hereupon of the forces of other nations which the Egyptians had in their pay is here foretold. Some considerable number of those troops, it is probable, were posted upon the frontiers to guard them, where they were beaten off by the invaders and put to flights. Then were the <hi type="italic">valiant men swept away</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.15">v. 15</reference>) as with <hi type="italic">a sweeping rain</hi> (it is the word that is used <reference osisRef="Prov.28.3">Prov. xxviii. 3</reference>); they can none of them stand their ground, <hi type="italic">because the Lord drives them</hi> from their respective posts; he drives them by his terrors; he drives them by enabling the Chaldeans to drive them. It is not possible that those should fix whom the wrath of God chases. He it was (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.16">v. 16</reference>) that <hi type="italic">made many to fall, yea,</hi> when their day shall come to fall, the enemy needs not throw them down, they shall <hi type="italic">fall one upon another,</hi> every man shall be a stumbling-block to his fellow, to his follower; nay, if God please, they shall be made to <hi type="italic">fall upon one another,</hi> they shall be made to <hi type="italic">fall upon one another, every man's sword</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">against his fellow. Her hired men,</hi> the troops Egypt has in he service, are indeed <hi type="italic">in the midst of her like fatted bullocks,</hi> lusty men, able bodied and high spirited, who were likely for action and promised to make their part good against the enemy; but <hi type="italic">they are turned back;</hi> their hearts failed them, and, instead of fighting, they have <hi type="italic">fled away together.</hi> How could they withstand their fate when <hi type="italic">the day of their calamity had come,</hi> the day in which God will visit them in wrath? Some think they are compared to fatted bullocks for their luxury; they had wantoned in pleasures, so that they were very unfit for hardships, and therefore turned back and could not stand. In this consternation, (1.) They all made homeward towards their own country (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">They said, "Arise, and let us go again to our own people,</hi> where we may be safe <hi type="italic">from the oppressing sword</hi> of the Chaldeans, that bears down all before it." In times of exigence little confidence is to be put in mercenary troops, that fight purely for pay, and have no interest in theirs whom they fight for. (2.) They exclaimed vehemently against Pharaoh, to whose cowardice or bad management, it is probably, their defeat was owing. When he posted them there upon the borders of his country it is probably that he told them he would within such a time come himself with a gallant army of his own subjects to support them; but he failed them, and, when the enemy advanced, they found they had none to back them, so that they were perfectly abandoned to the fury of the invaders. No marvel then that they quitted their post and deserted the service, crying out, <hi type="italic">Pharaoh king of Egypt is but a noise</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.17">v. 17</reference>); he can hector, and talk big of the mighty things he would do, but that is all; he brings nothing to pass. All his promises to those in alliance with him, or that are employed for him, vanish into smoke. He brings not the succours he engaged to bring, or not till it is too late: <hi type="italic">He has passed the time appointed;</hi> he did not keep his word, nor keep his day, and therefore they bid him farewell, they will never serve under him any more. Note, Those that make most noise in any business are frequently but a noise. Great talkers are little doers. <div eID="gen18132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18133" type="x-p"/> 3. The formidable power of the Chaldean army is here described as bearing down all before it. <hi type="italic">The King</hi> of kings, <hi type="italic">whose name is the Lord of hosts,</hi> and before whom the mightiest kings on earth, though gods to us, are but as grasshoppers, he hath said it, he hath sworn it, <hi type="italic">As I live, saith</hi> this <hi type="italic">king, as Tabor</hi> overtops <hi type="italic">the mountains and Carmel</hi> overlooks <hi type="italic">the sea, so shall</hi> the king of Babylon overpower all the force of Egypt, such a command shall he have, such a sway shall he bear, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.18">v. 18</reference>. He and his <hi type="italic">army shall come against</hi> Egypt <hi type="italic">with axes, as hewers of wood</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.22">v. 22</reference>), and the Egyptians shall be no more able to resist them than the tree is to resist the man that comes with an axe to <hi type="italic">cut it down;</hi> so that Egypt shall be felled as a <hi type="italic">forest</hi> is <hi type="italic">by the hewers of wood,</hi> which (if there by many of them, and those well provided with instruments for the purpose) will be done in a little time. Egypt is very populous, full of towns and cities, like a forest, the trees of which <hi type="italic">cannot be searched</hi> or numbered, and very rich, full of hidden treasures, many of which will escape the searching eye of the Chaldean soldiers; but they shall make a great spoil in the country, for <hi type="italic">they are more than the locusts,</hi> that come in vast swarms and overrun a country, devouring every green thing (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.6-Joel.1.7">Joel i. 6, 7</reference>), so shall the Chaldeans do, for <hi type="italic">they are innumerable.</hi> Note, The Lord of hosts hath numberless hosts at his command. <div eID="gen18133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18134" type="x-p"/> 4. The desolation of Egypt hereby is foretold, and the waste that should be made of that rich country. <hi type="italic">Egypt is</hi> now <hi type="italic">like a very fair heifer,</hi> or calf (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.20">v. 20</reference>), fat and shining, and not <hi type="italic">accustomed to the yoke</hi> of subjection, wanton as a heifer that is well fed, and very sportful. Some think here is an allusion to Apis, the bull or calf which the Egyptians worshipped, from whom the children of Israel learned to worship the golden calf. Egypt is as fair as a goddess, and adores herself, <hi type="italic">but destruction comes; cutting up comes</hi> (so some read it); <hi type="italic">it comes out of the north;</hi> thence the Chaldean soldiers shall come, as so many butchers or sacrificers, to kill and cut up this <hi type="italic">fair heifer.</hi> (1.) The Egyptians shall be brought down, shall be tamed, and their tune changed: <hi type="italic">The daughters of Egypt shall be confounded</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.24">v. 24</reference>), shall be filled with astonishment. <hi type="italic">Their voice shall go like a serpent,</hi> that is, it shall be very low and submissive; they shall not low like a fair heifer, that makes a great noise, but hiss out of their holes like serpents. They shall not dare to make loud complaints of the cruelty of the conquerors, but vent their griefs in silent murmurs. They shall not now, as they used to do, answer roughly, but, with <hi type="italic">the poor, use entreaties</hi> and beg for their lives. (2.) They shall be carried away prisoners into their enemy's land (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.19">v. 19</reference>): "<hi type="italic">O thou daughter! dwelling</hi> securely and delicately <hi type="italic">in Egypt,</hi> that fruitful pleasant country, do not think this will last always, but <hi type="italic">furnish thyself to go into captivity;</hi> instead of rich clothes, which will but tempt the enemy to strip thee, get plain and warm clothes; instead of fine shoes, provide strong ones; and inure thyself to hardship, that thou mayest bear it the better." Note, It concerns us, among all our preparations, to prepare for trouble. We provide for the entertainment of our friends, let us not neglect to provide for the entertainment of our enemies, nor among all our furniture omit furniture for captivity. The Egyptians must prepare to flee; for their cities shall be evacuated. Noph particularly <hi type="italic">shall be desolate, without an inhabitant,</hi> so general shall the slaughter and the captivity be. There are some penalties which, we say, the king and the multitude are exempted from, but here even these are obnoxious: <hi type="italic">The multitude of No shall be punished:</hi> it is called <hi type="italic">populous No,</hi> <reference osisRef="Nah.3.8">Nah. iii. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Though hand join in hand,</hi> yet they shall not escape; nor can any think to go off in the crowd. Be they ever so many, they shall find God will be too many for them. Their kings and all their petty princes shall fall; and their gods too (<reference osisRef="Jer.43.12-Jer.43.13">ch. xliii. 12, 13</reference>), their idols and their great men. Those which they call their tutelar deities shall be no protection to them. Pharaoh shall be brought down, and <hi type="italic">all those that trust in him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.25">v. 25</reference>), particularly the Jews that came to sojourn in his country, trusting in him rather than in God. All these shall be <hi type="italic">delivered into the hands of the northern nations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.24">v. 24</reference>), into the hand not only of Nebuchadnezzar that mighty potentate, but <hi type="italic">into the hands of his servants,</hi> according to the curse on Ham's posterity, of which the Egyptians were, that they should be the <hi type="italic">servants of servants.</hi> These seek their lives, and into their hands they shall be delivered. <div eID="gen18134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18135" type="x-p"/> 5. An intimation is given that in process of time Egypt shall recover itself again (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">Afterwards it shall be inhabited,</hi> shall be peopled again, whereas by this destruction it was almost dispeopled. Ezekiel foretels that this should be at the end of forty years, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.13">Ezek. xxix. 13</reference>. See what changes the nations of the earth are subject to, how they are emptied and increased again; and let not nations that prosper be secure, nor those that for the present are in thraldom despair. <div eID="gen18135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18136" type="x-p"/> II. Comfort and peace are here spoken to the Israel of God, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.27-Jer.46.28">v. 27, 28</reference>. Some understand it of those whom the king of Egypt had carried into captivity with Jehoahaz, but we read not of any that were carried away captives with him; it may therefore rather refer to the captives in Babylon, whom God had mercy in store for, or, more generally, to all the people of God, designed for their encouragement in the most difficult times, when the judgments of God are abroad among the nations. We had these words of comfort before, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.10-Jer.30.11">ch. xxx. 10, 11</reference>. 1. Let the wicked of the earth tremble, they have cause for it; <hi type="italic">but fear not thou, O my servant Jacob! and be not dismayed, O Israel!</hi> and again, <hi type="italic">Fear thou not, O Jacob!</hi> God would not have his people to be a timorous people. 2. The wicked of the earth <hi type="italic">shall be put away like dross,</hi> not be looked after any more; but God's people, in order to their being saved, shall be found out and gathered though they be far off, shall be redeemed though they be held fast in captivity, and shall return. 3. The wicked <hi type="italic">is like the troubled sea when it cannot rest;</hi> they <hi type="italic">flee when none pursues.</hi> But Jacob, being at home in God, <hi type="italic">shall be at rest and at ease, and none shall make him afraid;</hi> for <hi type="italic">what time he is afraid</hi> he has a <hi type="italic">God to trust to.</hi> 4. The wicked God <hi type="italic">beholds afar off;</hi> but, wherever thou art, <hi type="italic">O Jacob! I am with thee, a very present help.</hi> 5. A <hi type="italic">full end shall be made</hi> of the nations that oppressed God's Israel, as Egypt and Babylon; but mercy shall be kept in store for the Israel of God: they shall be corrected, but not cast off; the correction shall be in measure, in respect of degree and continuance. Nations have their periods; the Jewish nation itself has come to an end as a nation; but the gospel church, God's spiritual Israel, still continues, and will to the end of time; in that this promise is to have its full accomplishment, that, though God correct it, he will never <hi type="italic">make a full end of it.</hi>  <chapter eID="Jer.46"/> <div eID="gen18136" type="x-p"/>

entries.3a54b5dd8c93fa8b2a88a21a6c86093d2c305b3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10552"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 46</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.46.1-Jer.46.28">Jr 46:1-28</reference>. The Prophecies, Forty-sixth through Fifty-second Chapters, Refer to Foreign Peoples.</title> <div sID="gen18823" type="x-p"/> He begins with Egypt, being the country to which he had been removed. The forty-sixth chapter contains two prophecies concerning it: the discomfiture of Pharaoh-necho at Carchemish by Nebuchadnezzar, and the long subsequent conquest of Egypt by the same king; also the preservation of the Jews (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.27">Jr 46:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.28">28</reference>).<div eID="gen18823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18824" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10552"/>1. General heading of the next six chapters of prophecies concerning the Gentiles; the prophecies are arranged according to nations, not by the dates. <div eID="gen18824" type="x-p"/>
entries.db57a76ce83589135c49f7d6be30c42382fd3bab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10553"/><div sID="gen18825" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10553"/>2. Inscription of the first prophecy.<div eID="gen18825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18826" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Pharaoh-necho--</hi>He, when going against Carchemish (Cercusium, near the Euphrates), encountered Josiah, king of Judah (the ally of Assyria), at Megiddo, and slew him there (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.29">2Ki 23:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.20-2Chr.35.24">2Ch 35:20-24</reference>); but he was four years subsequently overcome at Carchemish, by Nebuchadnezzar, as is foretold here; and lost all the territory which had been subject to the Pharaohs west of the Euphrates, and between it and the Nile. The prediction would mitigate the Jews' grief for Josiah, and show his death was not to be unavenged (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.7">2Ki 24:7</reference>). He is famed as having fitted out a fleet of discovery from the Red Sea, which doubled the Cape of Good Hope and returned to Egypt by the Mediterranean. <div eID="gen18826" type="x-p"/>
entries.794429ef9cd11e73376fa9ebf00153049678851b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10554"/><div sID="gen18827" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10554"/>3. Derisive summons to battle. With all your mighty preparation for the invasion of Nebuchadnezzar, when ye come to the encounter, ye shall be "dismayed" (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.5">Jr 46:5</reference>). Your mighty threats shall end in nothing.<div eID="gen18827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18828" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">buckler--</hi>smaller, and carried by the light-armed cavalry.<div eID="gen18828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18829" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shield--</hi>of larger size, and carried by the heavily armed infantry. <div eID="gen18829" type="x-p"/>
entries.2aeb145f27396bd10276fbe86fc69834f955a821: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10555"/><div sID="gen18830" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10555"/><hi type="bold">4. Harness the horses--</hi>namely, to the war chariots, for which Egypt was famed (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.7">Ex 14:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.15.4">15:4</reference>).<div eID="gen18830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18831" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">get up, ye horsemen--</hi>get up into the chariots. Maurer, because of the parallel "horses," translates, "Mount the steeds." But it is rather describing the successive steps in equipping the war chariots; first harness the horses to them, then let the horsemen mount them.<div eID="gen18831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18832" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brigandines--</hi>cuirasses, or coats of mail. <div eID="gen18832" type="x-p"/>
entries.70f1c05c810932102d90281cc77c2d607ff793f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10556"/><div sID="gen18833" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10556"/>5. (See on <reference osisRef="Jer.46.3">Jr 46:3</reference>). The language of astonishment, that an army so well equipped should be driven back in "dismay." The prophet sees this in prophetic vision.<div eID="gen18833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18834" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fled apace--</hi>literally, "fled a flight," that is, flee precipitately.<div eID="gen18834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18835" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">look not back--</hi>They do not even dare to look back at their pursuers. <div eID="gen18835" type="x-p"/>
entries.cfe1cb5510c3276e4a4f099d1a598d284f9c66c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10557"/><div sID="gen18836" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10557"/><hi type="bold">6. Let not--</hi>equivalent to the strongest negation. Let not any of the Egyptian warriors think to escape by swiftness or by might.<div eID="gen18836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18837" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">toward the north--</hi>that is, in respect to Egypt or Judea. In the northward region, by the Euphrates (see <reference osisRef="Jer.46.2">Jr 46:2</reference>). <div eID="gen18837" type="x-p"/>
entries.7e2c144845f1447bc78d6491302f819fe30f061b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10558"/><div sID="gen18838" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10558"/><hi type="bold">7. as a flood--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.47.2">Jr 47:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.7">Is 8:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.22">Da 11:22</reference>). The figure is appropriate in addressing Egyptians, as the Nile, their great river, yearly overspreads their lands with a turbid, muddy flood. So their army, swelling with arrogance, shall overspread the region south of Euphrates; but it, like the Nile, shall retreat as fast as it advanced. <div eID="gen18838" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a815690f2874828e71a9913e97508ef0ecf047b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10559"/><div sID="gen18839" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10559"/>8. Answer to the question in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.7">Jr 46:7</reference>.<div eID="gen18839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18840" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">waters ... moved like the rivers--</hi>The rise of the Nile is gentle; but at the mouth it, unlike most rivers, is much agitated, owing to the sandbanks impeding its course, and so it rushes into the sea like a cataract. <div eID="gen18840" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e388a484a09eabdbae5f79c909540bcde8e592e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10560"/><div sID="gen18841" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10560"/>9. Ironical exhortation, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.3">Jr 46:3</reference>. The Egyptians, owing to the heat of their climate and abstinence from animal food, were physically weak, and therefore employed mercenary soldiers.<div eID="gen18841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18842" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ethiopians--</hi>Hebrew, Cush: Abyssinia and Nubia.<div eID="gen18842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18843" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Libyans--</hi>Phut, Mauritania, west of Egypt (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.10.6">Ge 10:6</reference>).<div eID="gen18843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18844" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shield--</hi>The Libyans borrowed from Egypt the use of the long shield extending to the feet [Xenophon, Cyropædia, 6 and 7].<div eID="gen18844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18845" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lydians--</hi>not the Lydians west of Asia Minor (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.22">Ge 10:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.5">Eze 30:5</reference>), but the Ludim, an African nation descended from Egypt (Mizraim) (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.13">Ge 10:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.5">Eze 30:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.3.9">Na 3:9</reference>).<div eID="gen18845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18846" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">handle and bend the bow--</hi>The employment of two verbs expresses the manner of bending the bow, namely, the foot being pressed on the center, and the hands holding the ends of it. <div eID="gen18846" type="x-p"/>
entries.ebe729b67fdc3024b3fe21f427bdd092cca27bde: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10561"/><div sID="gen18847" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10561"/><hi type="bold">10. vengeance--</hi>for the slaughter of Josiah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.29">2Ki 23:29</reference>).<div eID="gen18847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18848" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sword shall devour ... be ... drunk--</hi>poetical personification (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.42">De 32:42</reference>).<div eID="gen18848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18849" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a sacrifice--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.34.6">Is 34:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.39.17">Eze 39:17</reference>). The slaughter of the Egyptians is represented as a sacrifice to satiate His righteous vengeance. <div eID="gen18849" type="x-p"/>
entries.00b884c89ccf41f70dc5799cd3aa81050ea97eee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10562"/><div sID="gen18850" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10562"/><hi type="bold">11. Gilead ... balm--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Jer.8.22">Jr 8:22</reference>); namely, for curing the wounds; but no medicine will avail, so desperate shall be the slaughter.<div eID="gen18850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18851" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">virgin--</hi>Egypt is so called on account of her effeminate luxury, and as having never yet been brought under foreign yoke.<div eID="gen18851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18852" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou shalt not be cured--</hi>literally, "there shall be no cure for thee" (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.13">Jr 30:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.21">Eze 30:21</reference>). Not that the kingdom of Egypt should cease to exist, but it should not recover its former strength; the blow should be irretrievable. <div eID="gen18852" type="x-p"/>
entries.acfb2b176f59d9779d83cccf4dc24999d423e245: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10563"/><div sID="gen18853" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10563"/><hi type="bold">12. mighty ... stumbled against ... mighty ... fallen both together--</hi>Their very multitude shall prove an impediment in their confused flight, one treading on the other. <div eID="gen18853" type="x-p"/>
entries.efcba19398dcaa80d1de3785b67f5ea2a28f11ca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10564"/><div sID="gen18854" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10564"/>13-26. Prophecy of the invasion of Egypt by Nebuchadnezzar, which took place sixteen years after the taking of Jerusalem. Having spent thirteen years in the siege of Tyre, and having obtained nothing for his pains, he is promised by God Egypt for his reward in humbling Tyre (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.17-Ezek.20.30">Eze 29:17-20; 30</reference>:1-31:18). The intestine commotions between Amasis and Pharaoh-hophra prepared his way (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Isa.19.1">Is 19:1</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen18854" type="x-p"/>
entries.68dbdfb706f804aa16517656d88baf05a2f6b868: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10576"/><div sID="gen18885" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10576"/>27-28. Repeated from <reference osisRef="Jer.30.10">Jr 30:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.11">11</reference>. When the Church (and literal Israel) might seem utterly consumed, there still remains hidden hope, because God, as it were, raises His people from the dead (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.15">Ro 11:15</reference>). Whereas the godless "nations" are consumed even though they survive, as are the Egyptians after their overthrow; because they are radically accursed and doomed [Calvin]. <chapter eID="Jer.46"/>

entries.56d1b19f5ff1f74e5a1ecaf4c70e57dc16383511: <div eID="gen30517" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen30518" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30519" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30519" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30518" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30520" type="x-p"/> The difference between the preceding and the subsequent prophecies in point of composition is very remarkable; the last excelling much in majesty and elegance. This chapter (of which the first verse forms a general title to this and the five chapters following) contains two distinct prophecies relating to Egypt. The first was delivered previous to an engagement between Pharaoh-necho, king of Egypt, and Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon; in which the Egyptians were routed in Carchemish with great slaughter, as here predicted. The prophet sees the mighty preparations; but they are all declared to be of no avail, as God had decreed their fall, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.1-Jer.46.6">Jer 46:1-6</reference>. The King of Egypt, however, is represented as marching with all the confidence of victory, like a river overflowing its banks, and threatening all around with its inundation, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.7">Jer 46:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.8">Jer 46:8</reference>. But this immense armament of Pharaoh-necho, consisting of various nations, shall, by a righteous judgment of God, receive such a signal overthrow near the river Euphrates, that the political consequence of Egypt shall be thereby irretrievably ruined, and its remaining power become contemptible in the sight of the nations, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.9-Jer.46.12">Jer 46:9-12</reference>. The other prophecy, beginning at the thirteenth verse, relates to the memorable overthrow of the Egyptians by Nebuchadnezzar, subsequent to his siege of Tyre, in the sixteenth year after the destruction of Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.13-Jer.46.26">Jer 46:13-26</reference>. The promise, in the conclusion of the chapter, of preservation to the Jews, (who have for many ages continued a distinct people, when the various nations of antiquity who oppressed them, or with whom they had any intercourse, have long ago ceased to have any separate and visible existence), has been most remarkably fulfilled; and is a very signal act of providence, and a pledge of the restoration of Israel to the Divine favor, when the time of the Gentiles shall be fulfilled, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.27">Jer 46:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.28">Jer 46:28</reference>. <div eID="gen30520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30521" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen30521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30522" type="x-p"/> The word of the Lord - against the Gentiles - This is a general title to the following collection of prophecies, written concerning different nations, which had less or more connection with the Jews, either as enemies, neighbors, or allies. <div eID="gen30522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30523" type="x-p"/> They were not written at the same time; and though some of them bear dates, yet it would be difficult to give them any chronological arrangement. Dahler's mode of ascertaining the times of their delivery may be seen in the table in the introduction.
entries.4470e39bb02d890f872cc913044cc2a4850c60ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen30523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30524" type="x-p"/> Pharaoh-necho - This was the person who defeated the army of Josiah, in which engagement Josiah received a mortal wound, of which he died, greatly regretted, soon after at Megiddo. After this victory, he defeated the Babylonians, and took Carchemish; and, having fortified it, returned to his own country. Nabopolassar sent his son Nebuchadnezzar with an army against him, defeated him with immense slaughter near the river Euphrates, retook Carchemish, and subdued all the revolted provinces, according to the following prophecies.
entries.aae129cbf8142eadbbef7bd59f6d0721ef029d29: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen30524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30525" type="x-p"/> Order ye the buckler - This is the call to the general armament of the people against the Chaldeans.
entries.a369d2f13bec30f18096a536908f2cfc53d736e8: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen30525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30526" type="x-p"/> Furbish the spears - Cleanse, brighten, and sharpen them; from the Franco-Gallic fourbir, to polish, brighten. <div eID="gen30526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30527" type="x-p"/> Brigandines - A coat of mail, especially that which was made scale fashion; one plate overlapping the other, like the scales of fish.
entries.e254298e15d0cd7c699002ff3a291c471829eb79: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen30527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30528" type="x-p"/> Wherefore have I seen them dismayed - What! such a numerous, formidable, and well-appointed army panic-struck? So that they have turned back - fled apace, and looked not round; while their mighty ones - their generals and commanders, striving to rally them, are beaten down.
entries.bde41d40c78e5b33b8787215da4cf3c78904a52d: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen30528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30529" type="x-p"/> Let not the swift flee away - Even the swiftest shall not be able to escape. <div eID="gen30529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30530" type="x-p"/> They shall - fall toward the north - By the Euphrates, which was northward of Judea. Here the Egyptian army was routed with great slaughter.
entries.da1417a5e7c26f285d4f052326244aede1d0ce10: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen30530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30531" type="x-p"/> Who is this that cometh up as a flood - The vast concourse of people is here represented as a river: for instance, the Jordan, suddenly swollen with the rains in harvest, rolling its waters along, and overflowing the whole country. A fine image to represent the incursions of vast armies carrying all before them. Such was the army of Pharaoh-necho in its march to Carchemish.
entries.14d29034e6348f5e45b3a0dc570190cb62095b71: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen30531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30532" type="x-p"/> The Ethiopians - Hebrews Cush, Phut, and the Ludim. This army was composed of many nations. Cush. which we translate Ethiopians, almost invariably means the Arabians; and here, those Arabs that bordered on Egypt near the Red Sea. Phut probably means the Libyans; for Phut settled in Libya, according to Josephus. Phut and Cush were two of the sons of Ham, and brothers to Mitsraim, the father of the Egyptians, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.6">Gen 10:6</reference>; and the Ludim were descended from Mitsraim; see <reference osisRef="Gen.10.13">Gen 10:13</reference>. Bochart contends that the Ludim were Ethiopians, and that they were famous for the use of the bow. Phaleg, lib. 4:26.
entries.5653e6c83a79cb5068b5fa324d406280c9a42ca1: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen30532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30533" type="x-p"/> For this is the day of the Lord God of hosts - The prophet represents this as a mighty sacrifice, where innumerable victims were slain.
entries.2777420aa2657bd4c7f6a66993891f71de2e9517: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen30533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30534" type="x-p"/> Go up into Gilead, and take balm - An irony. Egypt is so completely enfeebled by this overthrow, that her political wound is utterly incurable. This figure is used with the more propriety here, as the Egyptians have been celebrated from the remotest antiquity for their knowledge of medicine.
entries.1d7d530decb21b78d2f3536c28305dd06e0cbdd9: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen30534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30535" type="x-p"/> The nations have heard of thy shame - Of thy disgrace, by this prodigious slaughter of thy troops.
entries.d9e5c21a5b9bf5ea34231ad948b24b278d80472a: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen30535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30536" type="x-p"/> How Nebuchadrezzar - should come and smite the land of Egypt - See on Jeremiah 44 (note). This was after Amasis had driven Pharaoh-necho into Upper Egypt. See <reference osisRef="Jer.44.30">Jer 44:30</reference>.
entries.6b5e42a19e484418e515b53929e41e26eba9d033: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen30536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30537" type="x-p"/> Migdol - Magdolum, a city of Lower Egypt. Noph, Memphis. Tahpanhes, Daphne. See before, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.1">Jer 44:1</reference> (note). <div eID="gen30537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30538" type="x-p"/> Round about thee - The Phoenicians, Philistines, Ammonites, Moabites, and Edomites, all prostrated by the arms of the Chaldeans.
entries.2016497b2d3a2c5cf36fc54b30c057a253151b92: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen30538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30539" type="x-p"/> They stood not, because the Lord did drive them - The Lord panic-struck them, and drove them back.
entries.f4c4e0426d29a83c8dfc557b28aae33d711ccb90: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen30539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30540" type="x-p"/> One fell upon another - In their terror and confusion ranks fell on ranks, and overturned each other. <div eID="gen30540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30541" type="x-p"/> Let us go again to our own people - Let us flee to our own country with all possible speed. These were the auxiliaries.
entries.eaa07da66f106883ddc90c6ba54b1b1657a3236a: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen30541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30542" type="x-p"/> They did cry there - Dr. Blayney translates this cry thus: - - "O Pharaoh, king of Egypt, A tumult hath frustrated the appointed meeting." <div eID="gen30542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30543" type="x-p"/> These allies sent their excuse to Pharaoh, that the disasters they had met with had prevented them from joining him as they had intended.
entries.28636bec6ff0b115475c9c8efcca6370b3272bba: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen30543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30544" type="x-p"/> As Tabor is among the mountains - This mountain is situated in the plain of Esdraelon in Galilee, on the confines of the tribes of Zebulun and Issachar, <reference osisRef="Jos.19.22">Jos 19:22</reference>. It stood by itself, separated from all the other mountains by deep valleys, and is the highest of the whole. <div eID="gen30544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30545" type="x-p"/> And as Carmel by the sea - Carmel is a mountain on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea, on the southern frontier of the tribe of Asher. Were the Egyptians as distinguished for valor and strength as the mountains Tabor and Carmel are for height among the other mountains in their vicinity, they should not be able to stand the shock of the Chaldean army.
entries.e308228e083a2bb702d8c94a126f8fda830f9540: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen30545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30546" type="x-p"/> Furnish thyself to go into captivity - The thing is unavoidable; prepare for this calamity.
entries.2a2e7489e61f4d57cd64846288deeb19100cd510: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen30546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30547" type="x-p"/> Egypt is like a very fair heifer - Fruitful and useful; but destruction cometh out of the north, from Chaldea. It may be that there is an allusion here to Isis, worshipped in Egypt under the form of a beautiful cow.
entries.bc9660a1dfd4a95c7487278e9c7830c3e0ce865a: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen30547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30548" type="x-p"/> Are fled away together - Perhaps there is a reference here to the case of a cow stung with gnats. She runs hither and thither not knowing where to go; so shall it be with this scattered people.
entries.97d24bed12839ff116d0be4df1e2f6e1ff496fb6: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen30548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30549" type="x-p"/> The voice - shall go like a serpent - See <reference osisRef="Isa.29.4">Isa 29:4</reference> (note), and the note there.
entries.2408cbc542697039d2a6f691b35ff0e176c4aa74: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen30549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30550" type="x-p"/> They shall cut down her forest - Supposed to mean her cities, of which Egypt had no fewer than one thousand and twenty.
entries.2aa54e45da7bf39bca6aacd6b03611791f1babe6: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen30550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30551" type="x-p"/> The hand or the people of the north - The Chaldeans.
entries.cf80b1ec22b26324883d1db7662fbe448e71e5fe: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen30551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30552" type="x-p"/> The multitude of No - אמון מנא Amon minno, the Amon of No, called by the Greeks Διοσπολις, or Jupiter's city. It was the famous Thebes, celebrated anciently for its hundred gates. Amon was the name by which the Egyptians called Jupiter, who had a famous temple at Thebes. <div eID="gen30552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30553" type="x-p"/> The word Pharaoh is twice repeated here; and Dr. Dahler thinks that one may design Pharaoh Hophrah, and the other Amasis, the new king.
entries.7442d23c2cab7205dd8eb197406df951a04b7a78: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen30553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30554" type="x-p"/> Afterward it shall be inhabited - That is, within forty years, as Ezekiel had predicted, <reference osisRef="Eze.29.13">Eze 29:13</reference>.
entries.28c0f0d631a46594c38d8f5a3ed5d7e802eb0594: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen30554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30555" type="x-p"/> Fear not - my servant Jacob - In the midst of wrath God remembers mercy. Though Judah shall be destroyed, Jerusalem taken, the temple burnt to the ground, and the people carried into captivity, yet the nation shall not be destroyed. A seed shall be preserved, out of which the nation shall revive.
entries.d0018aec3904400535e4d3093cbd01986beb0d71: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen30555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30556" type="x-p"/> I will make a full end of all the nations whither I have driven thee; but I will not make a full end of thee - The Jews still remain as a distinct people, while the Assyrians, Chaldeans, Egyptians, etc., are no more! <div eID="gen30556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30557" type="x-p"/> On this subject, I cannot withhold from my readers the following very judicious remarks of Bp. Newton, in his Dissertations on the Prophecies. "The preservation of the Jews through so many ages, and the total destruction of their enemies, are wonderful events; and are made still more wonderful by being signified beforehand by the spirit of prophecy, as particularly in the passage before us. Their preservation is really one of the most illustrious acts of Divine Providence. They are dispersed among all nations, yet not confounded with any. The drops of rain which fall, nay the great rivers which flow into the ocean, are soon mingled with and lost in that immense body of waters. And the same, in all human probability, would have been the fate of the Jews; they would have been mingled and lost in the common mass of mankind: but, on the contrary, they flow into all parts of the world, mix with all nations, and yet keep separate from all. They still live as a distinct people; and yet they nowhere live according to their own laws, nowhere elect their own magistrates, nowhere enjoy the full exercise of their religion. Their solemn feasts and sacrifices are limited to one certain place; and that hath been now for many ages in the hands of strangers and aliens, who will not suffer them to come thither. No people have continued unmixed so long as they have done; not only of those who have sent colonies into foreign countries, but even of those who have remained in their own country. The northern nations have come in swarms into the more southern parts of Europe: but where are they now to be discerned and distinguished? The Gauls went forth in great bodies to seek their fortune in foreign parts; but what traces or footsteps of them are now remaining any where? In France, who can separate the race of the ancient Gauls from the various other people who from time to time have settled there? In Spain, who can distinguish between the first possessors, the Spaniards, and the Goths and Moors, who conquered and kept possession of the country for some ages? In England, who can pretend to say certainly which families are derived from the ancient Britons, and which from the Romans, Saxons, Danes, and Normans? The most ancient and honorable pedigrees can be traced up only to a certain period; and beyond that there is nothing but conjecture and uncertainty, obscurity and ignorance. But the Jews can go up higher than any nation; they can even deduce their pedigree from the beginning of the world. They may not know from what particular tribe or family they are descended; but they know certainly that they all sprang from the stock of Abraham. And yet the contempt with which they have been treated, and the hardships they have undergone in almost all countries, should, one would think, have made them desirous to forget or renounce their original: but they profess it; they glory in it; and after so many wars, massacres, and persecutions, they still subsist; they are still very numerous. And what but a supernatural power could have preserved them in such a manner as no other nation upon earth has been preserved? Nor is the providence of God less remarkable in the destruction of their enemies, than in their own preservation. For, from the beginning, who have been the great enemies and oppressors of the Jewish nation, removed them from their own land, and compelled them into captivity and slavery? The Egyptians afflicted them much, and detained them in bondage several years. The Assyrians carried away captive the ten tribes of Israel; and the Babylonians, afterwards, the two remaining tribes of Judah and Benjamin. The Syro-Macedonians, especially Antiochus Epiphanes, cruelly persecuted them; and the Romans utterly dissolved the Jewish state, and dispersed the people so as that they have never been able to recover their city and country again. And where are now those great and famous monarchies, which in their turn subdued and oppressed the people of God? Are they not vanished as a dream; and not only their power, but their very names, lost in the earth? The Egyptians, Assyrians, and Babylonians were overthrown and entirely subjugated by the Persians; and the Persians, it is remarkable, were the restorers of the Jews as well as the destroyers of their enemies. The Syro-Macedonians were swallowed up by the Romans; and the Roman empire, great and powerful as it was, was broken into pieces by the incursions of the northern nations; while the Jews are subsisting as a distinct people at this day. And what a wonder of providence is it, that the vanquished should so many ages survive the victors; and the former be spread all over the world, while the latter are no more! Nay, not only nations have been punished for their cruelties to the Jews, but Divine vengeance has pursued even single persons who have been their persecutors and oppressors. The first-born of Pharaoh was destroyed; and he himself with his host, drowned in the sea. Nebuchadnezzar was stricken with madness, and the crown was transferred from his family to strangers. Antiochus Epiphanes and Herod died in great agonies, with ulcers and vermin issuing from them. Flaccus, governor of Egypt, who barbarously plundered and oppressed the Jews of Alexandria, was afterwards banished and slain; and Caligula, who persecuted the Jews for refusing to do Divine honors to his statue, was murdered in the flower of his age, after a short and wicked reign. But where are now, - since they have absolutely rejected the Gospel. and been no longer the peculiar people of God, - where are now such visible manifestations of a Divine interposition in their favor? The Jews would do well to consider this point; for, rightly considered, it may be an effectual means of opening their eyes, and of turning them to Christ our Savior." See Bp. Newton on the prophecies, dissert. 8 sect. 2. And see the notes on Ezekiel, where the calamities of these miserable people are largely detailed.  <chapter eID="Jer.46"/> <div eID="gen30557" type="x-p"/>

entries.5357f023ef72518fd85314a7798f9ae686042e8e: <reference osisRef="Jer.46.1-Jer.46.2">Jer 46:1-2</reference> <hi type="italic">Superscriptions</hi>. - <reference osisRef="Jer.46.1">Jer 46:1</reference> contains the title for the whole collection of prophecies regarding the nations (הגּוים, as contrasted with Israel, mean the heathen nations), Jer 46-51. As to the formula, "What came as the word of Jahveh to Jeremiah," etc., cf. the remarks on Jer 14:1. - In <reference osisRef="Jer.46.2">Jer 46:2</reference>, the special heading of this chapter begins with the word מצרים .למצרים is subordinated by ל to the general title, - properly, "with regard to Egypt:" cf. למואב, etc., <reference osisRef="Jer.48.1">Jer 48:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.1">Jer 49:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.7">Jer 49:7</reference>,<reference osisRef="Jer.49.23">Jer 49:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.28">Jer 49:28</reference>, also Jer 23:9. This chapter contains two prophecies regarding Egypt, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.2-Jer.46.12">Jer 46:2-12</reference>, and vv. 13-28. למצרים refers to both. After this there follows an account of the occasion for the first of these two prophecies, in the words, "Concerning the army of Pharaoh-Necho, the king of Egypt, which was at the river Euphrates, near Carchemish, which Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon smote in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah." נכו, as in <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.20">2Ch 35:20</reference>, or נכּה, as in 2Ki 23:29, in lxx Νεχαώ; Egyptian, according to Brugsch (<hi type="italic">Hist. d'Egypte</hi>, i. p. 252), <hi type="italic">Nekaaou</hi>; in Herodotus Νεκώς, - is said by Manetho to have been the sixth king of the twenty-sixth (Saïte) dynasty, the second Pharaoh of this name, the son of Psammetichus I, and grandson of Necho I. Brugsch says he reigned from 611 to 595 b.c. See on 2 Chr. 23:29. The two relative clauses are co-ordinate, i.e., אשׁר in each case depends on חיל. The first clause merely states where Pharaoh’s army was, the second tells what befall it at the Euphrates. It is to this that the following prophecy refers. Pharaoh-Necho, soon after ascending the throne, in the last year of Josiah’s reign (610 b.c.), had landed in Palestine, at the bay of Acre, with the view of subjugating Hither Asia as far as the Euphrates, and had defeated the slain King Josiah, who marched out against him. He next deposed Jehoahaz, whom the people had raised to the throne as Josiah’s successor, and carried him to Egypt, after having substituted Eliakim, the elder brother of Jehoahaz, and made him his vassal-king, under the name of Jehoiakim. When he had thus laid Judah under tribute, he advanced farther into Syria, towards the Euphrates, and had reached Carchemish on that river, as is stated in this verse: there his army was defeated by Nebuchadnezzar, in the fourth year of the reign of Jehoiakim (606 b.c.); see on 2Ki 23:29. <hi type="italic">Carchemish</hi> is Κιρκήσιον, <hi type="italic">Circesium</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Cercusium</hi> of the classical writers,<note placement="foot">See the opinion of Rawlinson in Smith’s <hi type="italic">Bible Dictionary</hi>, vol. i. p. 278. - Tr.</note> <div eID="gen14351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14352" type="x-p"/> Arabic <hi type="italic">karqi=si=yat</hi>, a fortified city at the junction of the Chebar with the Euphrates, built on the peninsula formed by the two rivers (Ammian. Marc. xxiii. 5, Procop. <hi type="italic">bell. Pers.</hi> ii. 5, and Marasç. under <hi type="italic">Karkesija</hi>). All that now remains of it are ruins, called by the modern Arabs <hi type="italic">Abu Psera</hi>, and situated on the Mesopotamian side of the Euphrates, where that river is joined by the Chebar (Ausland, 1864, S. 1058). This fortress was either taken, or at least besieged, by Necho. The statement, "in the fourth year of Jehoiakim," can be referred exegetically only to the time of the defeat of the Egyptians at Carchemish, or the year of the battle, and is actually so understood by most interpreters. No one but Niebuhr (<hi type="italic">Gesch. Ass. u. Babl.</hi> S. 59, 86, 370ff.) alters the date of the battle, which he places in the third year of Jehoiakim, partly from consideration of <reference osisRef="Dan.1.1">Dan 1:1</reference>, partly from other chronological calculations; he would refer the date given in our verse to the time when the following song was composed or published. But <reference osisRef="Dan.1.1">Dan 1:1</reference> does not necessarily require us to make any such assumption (see on that passage), and the other chronological computations are quite uncertain. Exegetically, it is as impossible to insert a period after "which Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon smote" (Nieb. p. 86, note 3), as to connect the date "in the fourth year of Jehoiakim" with "which word came to Jeremiah" (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.10">Jer 46:10</reference>). The title in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.1">Jer 46:1</reference> certainly does not refer specially to the prophecy about Egypt, but to על־הגּוים. But if we wished to make the whole of <reference osisRef="Jer.46.2">Jer 46:2</reference> dependent on 'אשׁר היה דבר , which would, at all events, be a forced, unnatural construction, then, from the combination of the title in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.1">Jer 46:1</reference> with the specification of time at the end of <reference osisRef="Jer.46.2">Jer 46:2</reference>, it would follow that all the prophecies regarding the nations had come to Jeremiah in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, - which would contradict what is said in the heading to the oracle against Elam (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.34">Jer 49:34</reference>), not to mention the oracle against Babylon. <div eID="gen14352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14353" type="x-p"/> Moreover, there is nothing to prevent us from assuming that the first prophecy against Egypt was revealed to Jeremiah, and uttered by him, in the same fourth year of Jehoiakim in which Necho was defeated by Nebuchadnezzar. In this way, the argument brought forward by Niebuhr in support of his forced interpretation, viz., that all specifications of time in the addresses of Jeremiah refer to the period of composition, loses all its force. In <reference osisRef="Jer.45.1">Jer 45:1</reference> also, and in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.9">Jer 51:9</reference>, the time when the event occurred coincides with the time when the utterance regarding it was pronounced. Although we assume this to hold in the case before us, yet it by no means follows that what succeeds, in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.3-Jer.46.12">Jer 46:3-12</reference>, is not a prophecy, but a song or lyric celebrating so important a battle, "the picture of an event that had already occurred," as Niebuhr, Ewald, and Hitzig assume. This neither follows from the statement in the title, "which Nebuchadnezzar in the fourth year of Jehoiakim smote," nor from the contents of the succeeding address. The superscription does not naturally belong to what Jeremiah has said or uttered, but must have been prefixed, for the first time, only when the address was committed to writing and inserted in the collection, and this not till after the battle had been fought; but it is evident that the address is to be viewed as substantially a prophecy (see <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Jer.46.6">Jer 46:6</reference></hi> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Jer.46.10">Jer 46:10</reference></hi>), although Jeremiah depicts, in the most lively and dramatic way, not merely the preparation of the mighty host, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.3">Jer 46:3</reference>, and its formidable advance, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.7-Jer.46.9">Jer 46:7-9</reference>, but also its flight and annihilation, in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.5">Jer 46:5</reference> and in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.10">Jer 46:10</reference>-12.
entries.580d14550c6252a193ec2a9ea053d1c615b3d0ac: <reference osisRef="Jer.46.3-Jer.46.4">Jer 46:3-4</reference> <hi type="italic">"Prepare shield and target, and advance to the battle. </hi> Jer 46:4. <hi type="italic">Yoke the horses [to the chariots]; mount the steeds, and stand with helmets on; polish the spears, put on the armour. </hi> Jer 46:5. <hi type="italic">Why do I see? they are terrified and turned back, and their heroes are beaten, and flee in flight, and do not turn: terror is round about, saith Jahveh. </hi> Jer 46:6. <hi type="italic">Let not the swift one flee, nor let the hero escape; towards the north, by the side of the river Euphrates, they stumble and fall. </hi> Jer 46:7. <hi type="italic">Who is this that cometh up like the Nile? his waters wave like the rivers. </hi> Jer 46:8. <hi type="italic">Egypt cometh up like the Nile, [his] waters are moved like the rivers; and he saith, I will go up, I will cover the earth; I will destroy the city, and those who dwell in it. </hi> Jer 46:9. <hi type="italic">Go up, ye horses; and drive furiously, ye chariots; and let the heroes go forth; Cushites and Phutites, bearing the shield; and Lydians, handling [and] bending the bow. </hi> Jer 46:10. <hi type="italic">But that day [belongs] to the Lord Jahveh of hosts, a day of vengeance for avenging Himself on His enemies: and the sword shall devour and be satisfied, and shall drink its fill of their blood; for the Lord Jahveh of hosts holdeth a slaying of sacrifices in the land of the north at the river Euphrates. </hi> Jer 46:11. <hi type="italic">Go up to Gilead, and take balsam, O virgin, daughter of Egypt: in vain hast thou multiplied medicines; cure there is none for thee. </hi> Jer 46:12. <hi type="italic">The nations have heard of thine ignominy, and thy cry hath filled the earth: for heroes stumble against heroes, both of them fall together."</hi> <div eID="gen14353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14354" type="x-p"/> This address falls into two strophes, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.3-Jer.46.6">Jer 46:3-6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.46.7">Jer 46:7</reference>-12. In both are depicted in a lively manner, first the advance of the Egyptian host to the battle, then their flight and destruction. The whole has been arranged so as to form a climax: in the first strophe, the admirable equipment of the armies, and their sudden flight and defeat, are set forth in brief sentences; in the second, there is fully described not merely the powerful advance of the host that covers the earth, but also the judgment of inevitable destruction passed on them by God: the reason for the whole is also assigned. Jer 46:3. In order to represent the matter in a lively way, the description begins with the call addressed to the army, to make ready for the battle. "Make ready shield and target," the two main pieces of defensive armour. מגן was the small [round] shield; צנּה, <hi type="italic">scutum</hi>, the large shield, covering the whole body. "Advance to the fight," i.e., go forward into the battle. Then the address turns to the several portions of the army: first to those who fight from chariots, who are to yoke the horses; then to the horsemen, to mount the steeds. פּרשׁים are not horsemen, but riding-horses, as in 1Ki 5:6; 1Ki 10:26; Eze 27:14. עלה is construed with the accus., as in Gen 49:4. The rendering given by Dahler and Umbreit, "Mount, ye horsemen," and that of Hitzig, "Advance, ye horsemen," are against the parallelism; and the remark of the last-named writer, that "Mount the steeds" would be רכבוּ, does not accord with 1Sa 30:17. Next, the address is directed to the foot-soldiers, who formed the main portion of the army. These are to take up their position with helmets on, to polish the spears, i.e., to sharpen them, and to put on the pieces of armour, in order to be arrayed for battle. מרק, to rub, polish, remove rust from the spear, and thereby sharpen it. סריון, here and in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.3">Jer 51:3</reference> for שׁריון, a coat of mail, pieces of armour.
entries.12e649a176e9c66ba372c9a2905c92a29c15f028: <reference osisRef="Jer.46.5-Jer.46.7">Jer 46:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen14354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14355" type="x-p"/> Thus well arrayed, the host advances to the fight; but suddenly the seer perceives the magnificent army terror-stricken, retreating, and breaking out into a disorderly flight. The question, "Why (wherefore) do I see?" points to the unexpected and incomprehensible turn in the progress of events. המּה חתּים is not an accus. dependent on ראיתי, but an independent clause: "What do I see? They are terror-stricken" (חתּים, terrified, broken-spirited through terror). יכּתּוּ, Hoph. from כּתת, to be broken, here and in <reference osisRef="Job.4.20">Job 4:20</reference> applied to persons. מנוס is added to the verb instead of the inf. abs., to give emphasis to the idea contained in the word; cf. Ewald, §281, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. מגור מסּביב .a , "horror, terror around" (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.6.25">Jer 6:25</reference>), is taken by Ewald as the reply of Jahveh to the question, "Wherefore is this? On every side there is danger;" and this is appropriately followed by the imperatives in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.6">Jer 46:6</reference>, "Let no one, then, attempt to flee; not one shall escape to Egypt, but they must fall at the Euphrates." The perfects כּשׁלוּ ונפלוּ are prophetic; the stumbling and falling are as certain as if they had already happened. The second strophe commences at Jer 46:7. The description begins anew, and that with a question of astonishment at the mighty host advancing like the Nile when it bursts its banks and inundates the whole country. יאר is the name of the Nile, taken from the Egyptian into the Hebrew language; cf. Gen. 41ff., <reference osisRef="Exod.1.22">Exo 1:22</reference>, etc. התגּעשׁ, dash about (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.22">Jer 5:22</reference>), wave backwards and forwards: the Hithpa. is here interchanged with the Hithpo. without any difference of meaning.
entries.b24f8747634b329e219d24a3e10592e98f8e1170: <reference osisRef="Jer.46.8-Jer.46.9">Jer 46:8-9</reference> brings the answer to the question of astonishment: "Egypt approaches, its hosts cover the land like the waves of the Nile, to destroy cities and men." On the form  אבידה (with א contracted from אא), cf.
